note: Encoding single, utf16le, utf16be or all; minimum length; the character class is alphanumeric plus punctuation (the default, CyberChef's first choice, with the same punctuation) or printable (space to tilde), with a null-terminated switch instead of CyberChef's third class; the Unicode (non-ASCII) classes are not offered; display total, sort and unique as in CyberChef (unique keeps the first appearance, then sort, then the total). The UTF-16 zero bytes and a null terminator are not part of the output (CyberChef leaves them in). Input is read as bytes.

IPv4, IPv6 and remove-local as in CyberChef (the local ranges are 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 and 127/8); display total, sort and unique. Forge's own patterns: leading zeros are accepted, an address that is part of a longer dotted number is not found, IPv6 is found in all the forms of RFC 4291 (CyberChef finds only the full eight-group form and its simple shortenings), and the sort is by code point.
Forge's own pattern, ASCII only: quoted local parts and non-ASCII (internationalised) addresses are not found, and a host needs two or more labels.
Colon and hyphen forms as in CyberChef, plus the dotted Cisco form; a match inside a longer run of hex pairs is not found.

Any scheme with ://, user information, IPv6 hosts in brackets; trailing punctuation and unpaired closing brackets are left out, round brackets in pairs stay. Forge's own pattern, so edge cases differ from CyberChef's.

Forge's own pattern with CyberChef's Underscore option (off by default: a label with an underscore is then not part of a name). The option to show only valid top-level domains is not offered (it needs the list of top-level domains): the last label only has to be letters (or xn--), so file names such as report.txt are found too. A name after a dot or inside a longer word is not read from its middle (CyberChef finds example.com in _dmarc.example.com).

Windows and UNIX switches as in CyberChef. Forge's own patterns: a Windows folder name may hold single spaces but the last name stops at the first space; a UNIX path ends at white space and is not found inside a word, a URL or a relative path.

A length from 1 to 128 hex digits (40 by default), or all, which finds the digest sizes 4, 8, 16, 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 80, 96 and 128 digits with the values of each size together, the shortest size first, as CyberChef does (CyberChef also takes runs of 1 and 2 digits as hashes, which Forge does not); a run must not touch other letters, digits or underscores.

RAKE of Rose et al. 2010 with Forge's own English stop list (replaceable by a comma or white space separated list), a maximum phrase length (3 by default; CyberChef has none) instead of regular-expression delimiters, and a limit. The output is one line per phrase: its score (two decimals), a colon, a space and the phrase, highest score first, equal scores in alphabetical order. CyberChef writes Scores: , Keywords: , then score, phrase lines with the scores as plain numbers, and keeps punctuation attached to the words (so strict inequations, and strict inequations are different phrases there); Forge's words are letters, digits and marks with an inner apostrophe or hyphen, and every other character ends a phrase, so the keywords and scores differ.
